item.title: The Boy Who Stole Billions: what the first two episodes show about effective altruism and earning to give
item.description:
Published on November 17, 2026 12:20 AM GMT

I watched the first two episodes of The Boy Who Stole Billions, an upcoming Amazon series directed by Nanette Burstein about the convicted fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried, shown as a world premiere at DOC NYC.

In 2022, during the FTX scandal, I had never heard of effective altruism, and I barely remember the scandal itself. Today I encourage people to use EA principles for their careers and their giving, so I regularly get questions about it. The first impressions below are my own; the full summary of the two episodes was mostly written with AI. I’m writing in a personal capacity.

This post doesn’t aim to impose a reading of the series, and it isn’t a guide to answering questions on the topic. For that, the Centre for Effective Altruism’s post by @Tess Newton-Palmer on how to talk about the other FTX series, Netflix’s The Altruists (quite a month for TV shows on this topic) may be more useful for you. 


TL;DR: Effective altruism is at the heart of most of the first episode. The series seems to aim at reflecting reality without painting a very negative picture of EA. It shows that earning to give is what led Sam into this sector, and also that some of the effective altruists who worked with him early on, Tara Mac Aulay in particular, pushed for more prudence and for keeping promises to investors. Over the first two episodes, Sam comes across increasingly as a gambler, more and more detached from his initial altruistic goals.

What I took from the episodes: the gambler and the EAs who pushed back

The series presents Sam as a utilitarian loner and gambler inspired by earning to give, but it also lets other voices inspired by effective altruism be heard.

Earning to give at the root of the story

My view is that the series doesn’t stray far from reality. Even though effective altruism is mostly seen through the lens of earning to give, it is directly what led Sam into this sector. The documentary leans quite heavily on EA, with several excerpts from EA conference talks, notably by Will MacAskill, whose role in Sam’s path is well documented.

There is also the testimony of Tara Mac Aulay, former CEO of the Centre for Effective Altruism and co-founder of Alameda Research. Even though she helped Sam get into crypto and co-founded the company with him, I’d say she represents effective altruism well, because she is clearly one of the sane and ethical people featured in the documentary. She explains the disagreements over risk management and business ethics, and what led her to leave.

The documentary doesn’t paint the worst possible picture of SBF (I was surprised by some of the choices, which, to me, cast a somewhat a neutral, or even somewhat positive, light on someone who committed such a massive fraud). It begins with his childhood and includes testimony from his parents. Sam also describes his anhedonia, his inability to feel pleasure or joy. It also builds a narrative of Sam as a very isolated person who makes extremely dangerous decisions.

The early EAs depicted as the voice of reason

Some members of the EA community worked for Sam in the early days. They didn’t support his decisions and tried to oppose him and slow him down: take fewer risks, test before launching, don’t break promises to investors. When decisions became far too dangerous, they judged that this was not acceptable and chose to leave. Tara and others gave Sam an ultimatum, he refused, and around half the company left. This part relies mostly on Tara’s account, and Sam gets to give his side.

So in this first episode, members of the EA community are both the people who said “making a lot of money to give it away is good” and the people who tried to bring back reason and a careful use of funds.

The series also shows that, as Sam became famous, the community put him on a pedestal, even though, according to Tara, Alameda had made no donations during her time there. She says Sam warned her that the community would believe his version over hers. She describes feeling vulnerable after leaving, with her place in the EA community and her whole social life at stake, and starting to doubt herself as the community held him up as a model.

Altruistic motivations, then a drift

As the series tells it, the initial motivations are clear: these are very altruistic people, Sam included. Around him are people who want to have a positive impact: Tara; Wayne Hsiung, an animal rights activist active on the EA Forum, who pushed back against earning to give; and later Nishad Singh, an early Alameda employee who went on to head engineering at FTX, who complains that they still haven’t started giving.

After the split, the company turns more and more towards people willing to take risks. Most of the new hires were not looking to have an impact; they just wanted to get rich. While the first people involved were, perhaps, altruists, FTX became a money-maximising operation.

Sam keeps reasoning in terms of expected value, for instance arguing that a 20% chance of FTX not being a flop is enough to justify it. Yet none of the people depicted as effective altruists in the series makes this kind of argument, and by then most of the early ones have left. In a way, they come across as the voice of reason. Through Tara’s voice, effective altruism is associated with prudence and with the importance of keeping promises and not deceiving people.

Over the two episodes, Sam goes further and further in pursuit of more money, more profit, without starting to give significantly, and seems more and more detached from any altruistic goal. My personal impression is of a gambler going double or nothing every three months; what the series shows is Sam’s growing delusions of grandeur. The series also points out how little was donated compared with the company’s valuation, criticises the investment in a coal-powered mine on climate grounds, and shows the money spent on advertising. In the show’s narrative, all of this seems tied to the delusions of grandeur Sam develops as the episodes go on.

The relationship with Caroline

His relationship with Caroline Ellison is at the heart of the second episode. The episode ends with the first signs of trouble in Alameda’s management: the firm relies mostly on its own assets, which are far too unstable.

Summary of episodes 1 and 2

This summary of the two episodes was mostly written with AI.

Episode 1: from effective altruism to Alameda

The episode opens at the FTX Crypto Bahamas conference, with celebrities and former world leaders on stage, then cuts to the collapse: Sam Bankman-Fried was found guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy, about $8 billion of customer money is gone, and victims describe their losses. Sam takes part in the series through video calls from federal prison, limited to about 15 minutes a day. He says he wants “to get the truth out there”, even though the truth “has not been kind” to him.

Childhood and early ideas. Sam grows up near Stanford, where both his parents teach law. His parents describe a quiet, introverted child who didn’t fit in and responded to logic more than emotion. At a summer maths camp he meets Sam Trabucco and Gary Wang, who both play a role later. Trabucco remembers a teenager already talking about utilitarianism and expected value.

Discovering effective altruism. As a student at MIT, Sam finds the early EA community through an online forum and feels, for the first time, that he is not alone. Tara Mac Aulay explains the basic ideas: give 10% of your income and find the charities that do the most good per dollar. The series includes archive footage from EA talks, including a debate in which Will MacAskill says that, between saving a child or a Picasso from a burning building, he would save the Picasso and sell it to save many more children. Sam is drawn above all to animal welfare. Wayne Hsiung, an animal rights activist, remembers a young man who cared about neither wealth nor status. Will MacAskill suggests earning to give in finance. Hsiung thinks this would be a waste, but Sam follows MacAskill’s advice: he sees himself as bad at outreach and good at maths.

Jane Street. Sam joins Jane Street, a top trading firm where trading feels like a game. He donates six figures a year, feels no joy, and after an EA conference starts asking whether he could do more good elsewhere. With Tara, then CEO of the Centre for Effective Altruism, he maps out his options on a whiteboard. Tara shows him large price gaps for Bitcoin between exchanges. Sam, sceptical of crypto at first, realises it could be a huge trading opportunity and leaves Jane Street.

Founding Alameda Research. Sam and Tara found Alameda Research in 2017. All the equity is put in Sam’s name. Tara accepts because, as EAs, they plan to donate all profits anyway. Gary Wang builds the trading software, the team lives and works in a chaotic house in Berkeley, and investors from the EA community lend between $1 million and $100 million each, with a high level of trust because the profits are meant for charity. Nishad Singh, an EA and vegan who wanted to earn to give, joins; his wife describes his ambition and kindness. A trade between Japanese and US Bitcoin prices brings in around a million dollars a day. Tara explains that when a few thousand dollars can save a life, it becomes very hard to stop working.

Crisis and split. In early 2018 the crypto market crashes and wipes out most of the profits. Tara worked herself into the hospital. Around $15 million of crypto appears to be missing; Sam says later it was an accounting error and was recovered. The key conflict concerns a new trading bot: Tara wants it tested first, Sam agrees at a meeting with the lenders not to launch it untested, then switches it on the next day. Tara sees this as breaking a promise that put the investors’ money at risk. She also links Sam’s appetite for risk to his anhedonia, his inability to feel pleasure or joy, which he describes himself. Tara and part of the team try to buy him out and give him an ultimatum. He refuses, declares them fired, and about half the company leaves.

Sam loses most of his friends and roommates. He notes that the wider EA community took no formal position on who was right. Tara says Sam made clear that, as a rich, well-connected white man, his version would be believed over hers. She felt her place in the community, and her whole social life, were at risk. As Sam becomes a media figure, she starts to doubt herself, especially as the EA community holds him up as a model, although Alameda had made no donations while she was there. Archive footage shows MacAskill citing Sam’s success as proof that people can aim for even greater impact.

Episode 2: the relationship with Caroline and the rise of FTX

Hong Kong and new hires. Sam says he wanted to put distance between himself and the EA community to avoid a wider split, and moves Alameda to Hong Kong, then the centre of the crypto world. He recruits Sam Trabucco, who was not into effective altruism and wanted to get rich. Trabucco explains that the EAs who left were uncomfortable with almost any risk, and Sam wanted experienced traders. Caroline Ellison, a former Jane Street trader who shares Sam’s maths and EA background, also joins. Trabucco and Caroline soon run Alameda together. Sam and Caroline begin a relationship, largely through long written exchanges, which Sam insists on keeping secret.

Founding FTX. Sam decides to build a crypto exchange because exchanges earn fees on every trade. He reasons that a 20% chance of it not being a flop is enough to justify the bet. Gary Wang codes the first version. At a conference in Taiwan in 2019, Binance’s CEO, CZ, agrees to invest, which gives FTX credibility. Ryan Salame joins: he found the EA side “nuts” but opened his network to Sam. The pandemic triggers a crypto boom. FTX launches its own token, FTT, which is worth about $350 million on its first day. Sam says creating it took “a click of a button”.

Image and spending. The team builds Sam’s public persona: shorts, free T-shirts, the genius billionaire who will give everything away. Journalists, including those who put him in the Time 100, buy into it. FTX spends heavily on marketing, including deals with Tom Brady and Gisele Bündchen and $135 million for the naming rights to the Miami Heat’s arena. Nishad is increasingly uncomfortable with the spending. When CZ blocks new investors unless he is bought out, Sam buys back his stake with cash and around $600 million in FTT, a payment the series presents as decisive for what comes next.

The Bahamas. FTX moves to the Bahamas. Ryan Salame describes about half a billion dollars of real estate, charter flights for packages and a $30 million penthouse where Sam lives with about ten colleagues, including Caroline, Nishad and his wife. Sam explains that communal living helped him feel less lonely. Nishad’s wife describes a sense of mentorship from Sam. Salame describes vegan dinners where everyone flattered Sam.

Caroline. Caroline wants their relationship to be public; Sam refuses and puts the company first. The series reads out her own messages about feeling unloved and unsure of the relationship. Tension grows over Sam’s venture investments, which Caroline sees as a distraction. They break up, and working together becomes very difficult.

Giving and drift. Sam’s fortune is estimated at over $20 billion and he says he wants to give it away, but donations stay in the hundreds of millions, around $150 million against a $40 billion valuation. Nishad asks when they will really start giving. Salame and Zane Tackett visit a coal-powered crypto mining site in Kazakhstan; Sam invests anyway. Alameda makes about $5 billion of venture investments, including Anthropic, Solana and a stake in Robinhood. Nishad becomes the constant naysayer. Staff describe burnout and the open use of stimulants. Sam Trabucco quits Alameda, exhausted, leaving Caroline, Sam’s ex-partner, in charge.

Washington and the conflict of interest. To win a licence for margin trading in the US, Sam lobbies in Washington and becomes one of the biggest political donors in the midterms. He clashes with CZ, whom he reportedly described as close to the Chinese government. He says publicly that Alameda and FTX are separate, while his past relationship with Caroline, who runs Alameda, stays hidden.

The ending. A CoinDesk reporter obtains Alameda’s balance sheet: around 40% of its assets are in FTT, the token FTX created. The episode ends on the first doubts about Alameda’s financial health, and Sam says he believes Caroline leaked the document.

I hope this new spotlight on Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX won’t discourage people from using reason and evidence to do good in the world. The world faces huge problems, and we need people who take altruism seriously. The effective altruism community and the resources it has built can help them do that.

item.title: Where I Am Donating in 2026
item.description:
Published on November 16, 2026 9:29 PM GMT

I didn't want to spend 200 hours deciding where to donate like I did last year. Therefore, there are some promising orgs that I did not take the time to learn more about, and this writeup doesn't provide as much detail as 2024 or 2025. But I'll try to cover the big stuff.

Cross-posted from my website.

Cause prioritization

I explained my thinking in detail in 2024, and some changes to my beliefs in 2025. My high-level prioritization has not changed in 2026:

  • The top priority is to prevent misaligned AI from killing everyone.
  • The best way to do that is a global halt on frontier AI development.
  • At the margin, the best things to do are public and political advocacy to push for a global halt.

Since 2025, I've written some posts that add color to my views, including:

  • I'm extremely worried that superintelligent AI will kill everyone — the basic case for why I care about AI risk. Not a new belief, but it's the first time I've straightforwardly put it into writing.
  • Worlds where we solve AI alignment on purpose don't look like the world we live in — a collection of reasons why things look grim.
  • Pausing AI Is the Best Answer to Post-Alignment Problems — even if we solve alignment, there are a lot of ways the future could go badly; a moratorium on superintelligence seems like the best response.

(There are more relevant posts in the archive, especially under the "Existential Risk" and "Far Future" headings.)

A lot happened since last year, but not much that changed my priorities

This year:

  • Frontier AI has made huge improvements on certain cognitive tasks like math, even solving a Millennium Prize problem.
  • Anthropic's AI systems may be significantly accelerating its AI R&D, which suggests we may be on the brink of recursive self-improvement. We may be very close to the point of no return.
  • The Hugging Face incident was the first (and possibly last) "warning shot", where an AI system went rogue and caused real-world damage. The incident woke a lot of people up to the dangers of advanced AI.
  • Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic, and his resignation went unexpectedly viral and received a lot of media attention.

This all matters a lot, but it doesn't really change my prioritization. Here's how it did change my beliefs:

  • I have higher credence that pausing AI is urgent.
  • I'm more optimistic about our chances of achieving a global moratorium on AI development—the issue is both more popular and more salient.[1]
  • I'm less optimistic that things will miraculously work out somehow (e.g., it turns out alignment is easy, all you have to do is pick the right model persona or whatever). The window for a miracle is rapidly closing, and we're getting increasing evidence that current alignment techniques are not going to work.

Basically, 2026 has made me more confident in my preferred strategy of "advocate for a global ban on ASI".

There are more orgs working toward that goal (and doing advocacy toward that goal) than there were a year ago, but still not many orgs, so the cause remains neglected.

Post-alignment problems remain under-rated, but I don't see standout funding opportunities

By "post-alignment problems", I refer to the existential-scale problems that AI could bring even if we solve the alignment problem. Achieving an ideal future requires solving some critical problems, and it's not at all obvious that these problems can be deferred to AI.

Pausing AI is the best answer to post-alignment problems, but not necessarily the most cost-effective thing to work on.

  • I'm pessimistic about most relevant research agendas—I explained why in We won't solve post-alignment problems by doing research.

  • I'd like to see more work on post-ASI non-human welfare; I wrote about this here. There are a few orgs working on this and they get very little funding right now. However, I'm concerned that none of them take ASI sufficiently seriously, and their strategies will not scale to ASI (see The Future Will Be Weirder Than That).

  • Orgs like Compassion Aligned Machine Learning (CaML) work to improve AI's concern for sentient welfare. Will that work scale to superintelligence? We’re the co-founders of Better Futures Guide (BFG), a charity evaluator specifically focused on livelihoods. The program has been independently evaluated in a randomized controlled trial (Mahmud and Riley, 2026).[13] The researchers randomly assigned 335 villages and surveyed 3,852 households. About three years after the program began, the trial found the following economic effects in program villages:

  • Wealth in livestock, savings and household goods was 31% higher.
  • Consumption (what a household eats and uses) was 10% higher just after harvest, and 39% higher in the “lean season”, the months leading up to a harvest when food stores run low and households are hungriest.

These gains showed up in daily life. In the lean season, 25% of households in villages without the program said a child had gone to bed hungry during the past month. In program villages, it was 4%. For adults, the figures were 38% and 6%.

Gains reached households at every level. We have published an interactive, schematic version of our CEA on our website, where you can adjust our assumptions and see the effect on our estimate.

Our CEA has five main components:

  • Persistence. The trial followed households for about three years. We model seven scenarios for how long the effect lasts beyond that, each weighted by how well it fits the program’s design, its own monitoring data and long-run studies of other graduation programs.
  • Applicability. We adjust the trial’s results for each country, to reflect changes to the program since the trial and differences between Uganda, where the trial took place, and the other three countries.   • Cost. We take Raising The Village’s projected cost per participant in 2027–28 in each of its four countries, adjusted upward because, across organizations in general, actual costs tend to exceed projections.
  • Simulations. We run our model 10,000 times, each time drawing a different plausible value for every uncertain input. Founders Pledge and The Life You Can Save already recommend it, and GiveWell has published a back-of-the-envelope calculation (BOTEC) and is funding further research into its impact.[17] However, to our knowledge, we are the first evaluator to publish an extensive cost-effectiveness analysis of it, based on the most recent academic evidence.

Alongside cost-effectiveness, we assess room for more funding and organizational capacity, including ability to scale.

In addition to our poverty graduation work, the next sectors we’ll release recommendations in are foundational learning and cross-border livelihoods.

Raising The Village reached 647,000 people in 2025, 1 million in 2026, and aims to reach about 2 million in 2027. As it grows, it is testing how the program performs in new settings and with new partners. In Rwanda and the DRC, it is currently running deliberately small programs, which it calls Learning Hubs. In Tanzania, its activities launched this year.

Impact

The program has been independently evaluated in a randomized controlled trial (Mahmud and Riley, 2026).[13] The researchers randomly assigned 335 villages and surveyed 3,852 households. About three years after the program began, the trial found the following economic effects in program villages:

  • Income was 26% higher. About half of the gain came from selling more crops, and a third from more households running small businesses.
  • Wealth in livestock, savings and household goods was 31% higher.
  • Consumption (what a household eats and uses) was 10% higher just after harvest, and 39% higher in the “lean season”, the months leading up to a harvest when food stores run low and households are hungriest.

These gains showed up in daily life. In the lean season, 25% of households in villages without the program said a child had gone to bed hungry during the past month. In program villages, it was 4%. For adults, the figures were 38% and 6%.

Gains reached households at every level. The poorest quarter of households gained about as much in dollars as other households, which meant their gain was larger in proportion: their income was 41% higher than that of the poorest quarter of households in comparison villages. Serving every household did not come at the expense of those with the least.

These results are similar to the average effect of graduation programs in the recent meta-analysis, yet at about a third of the median cost of programs started since 2016[14].  Because of this notable cost-effectiveness, we have taken extra care to verify the plausibility of Mahmud and Riley’s results. Our conclusion, based on the trial’s quality, the wider graduation literature, and outside experts, is that we find the trial’s results plausible. 

Also, in addition to its whole-village model being lower-cost than household-based targeting,[15] we found Raising The Village to be an exceptionally data-driven organization. Its Annual Household Survey follows a random sample of households in each program village from baseline through year five, with the same survey administered in comparable non-program villages; its 2025 Impact Report draws on about 42,000 households in 1,575 villages. Leadership reviews program data quarterly and decides on changes for the following quarter. In 2024, for example, after cohort data showed consistently low income from perennial crops such as coffee, it introduced training in their cultivation. In the first cohort trained, Raising The Village’s monitoring data show per-household income from perennials rising from $23 at baseline to $102 a year later.

Cost-effectiveness

As part of our evaluation, we built a cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) of Raising The Village: a model that estimates the impact of a donation made in 2027 or 2028 relative to its cost. We measure impact in consumption doublings: one doubling is the equivalent of doubling one person’s consumption for one year.

Our findings:

  • Raising The Village achieves one consumption doubling for an estimated $27.

  • It is ~6x as cost-effective as cash transfers from GiveDirectly, on an estimated like-for-like basis.[16]

  • By our calculations, that is ~11x GiveWell’s benchmark, excluding health impacts that we did not model but that Raising The Village is likely to cause.

We have published an interactive, schematic version of our CEA on our website, where you can adjust our assumptions and see the effect on our estimate.

Our CEA has five main components:

  • Effect. We take the randomized trial’s effect on household consumption, measured separately just after harvest and in the months before the next one, when the effect was nearly four times larger. We then adjust both figures to account for the limits of evidence from a single trial.
  • Persistence. The trial followed households for about three years. We model seven scenarios for how long the effect lasts beyond that, each weighted by how well it fits the program’s design, its own monitoring data and long-run studies of other graduation programs.
  • Applicability. We adjust the trial’s results for each country, to reflect changes to the program since the trial and differences between Uganda, where the trial took place, and the other three countries. We also subtract the value that government contributions to the program would have had elsewhere.
  • Cost. We take Raising The Village’s projected cost per participant in 2027–28 in each of its four countries, adjusted upward because, across organizations in general, actual costs tend to exceed projections.
  • Simulations. We run our model 10,000 times, each time drawing a different plausible value for every uncertain input. The four inputs that move our estimate most are how long the effect lasts, the size of the effect in the months before harvest, how well the trial’s results apply to the program as it runs today. We have built each of these into the model. In 80% of our simulations, the cost per consumption doubling fell between $16 and $62, with half falling below about $30. Raising The Village was more cost-effective than our like-for-like GiveDirectly estimate in more than 99% of our simulations.

We are not the first evaluator to look at Raising The Village. Founders Pledge and The Life You Can Save already recommend it, and GiveWell has published a back-of-the-envelope calculation (BOTEC) and is funding further research into its impact.[17] However, to our knowledge, we are the first evaluator to publish an extensive cost-effectiveness analysis of it, based on the most recent academic evidence.

Room for more funding and organizational capacity

Alongside cost-effectiveness, we assess room for more funding and organizational capacity, including ability to scale.

With regards to funding, Raising The Village reported a funding gap of between $8 million and tens of millions of dollars a year in the growth scenarios it shared with us, and our full evaluation indicates it can use additional donations at the cost-effectiveness we have modeled.

Raising The Village is scaling quickly and aims to reach about 2 million people in 2027, up from 647,000 in 2025. This kind of growth will require it to adapt its management structure, among other things. Its growth also relies on increased government involvement, which can pose risks for implementation fidelity. In our full technical report, we discuss why we believe that Raising The Village can sustain the cost-effectiveness we have modeled as it grows.  

If you’d like to donate

You can donate to Raising The Village here. If you are considering a larger gift or advise donors, we’re happy to discuss our research further: info@betterfuturesguide.org.

Next steps for Better Futures Guide

In addition to our poverty graduation work, the next sectors we’ll release recommendations in are foundational learning and cross-border livelihoods.

We’re constantly looking for ways to maximize our own impact, and we welcome ideas, feedback, and proposals for collaboration. We’d also be grateful for introductions to funders and advisors who are active in this space. Please reach out to us at info@betterfuturesguide.org.

Better Futures Guide has received funding from the Livelihood Impact Fund (LIF), which is Raising The Village’s largest funder. We conduct our work independently from LIF, although its staff has provided us with valuable input and feedback.

We use Claude to assist our research and drafting process. All views, and the primary and final drafting of this post, are ours.

item.title: $1,000 Giving Summit: Breaking Out of the EA Bubble
item.description:
Published on November 17, 2026 4:48 PM GMT

On December 7–8,  Yield & Spread is hosting The $1,000 Giving Summit, a free, two-day podcast style event bringing together more than 15 influential voices from the personal finance and charitable giving communities to discuss how to make generosity a permanent part of our financial plans.

To my knowledge, this is the first time that this many personal finance pros have come together around this topic. 

The goal is to introduce a mainstream personal finance audience to the ideas of effective giving.

Why now?

Starting in 2026, Americans who take the standard deduction can deduct up to $1,000 in qualifying charitable contributions ($2,000 for married couples filing jointly). Previously, charitable deductions were only available to those who itemized, meaning the tax benefits of giving largely went to wealthier households or those willing to navigate the complexities of itemizing their deductions.

With roughly 90% of Americans taking the standard deduction, this creates a timely opportunity to get more people thinking about charitable giving.

We want to use this tax change as a starting point for a much bigger conversation about generosity, particularly within the Financial Independence world, where people already think deeply about building wealth but don't always talk about what they can do with it.

Who's speaking?

We're bringing together some of the biggest names in personal finance, including:

Mr. Money Mustache: He’s donated hundred of thousands of dollars to GiveWell
Money with Katie: She donates ⅓ of her podcast proceeds to charity
Jim Dahle of The White Coat Investor: 10% pledge-taker
Frank Vasquez of Risk Parity Radio: Also 10% pledge-taker!

They're joined by experts in charitable giving and research, including:

Carolien Teti of GiveDirectly:  They’re offering a 1.5x match as part of the summit
James Rayton of Giving What We Can:  The Index Funds of Giving 
Lara Aknin of the World Happiness Report: Does giving actually make us happy?
Larissa MacFarquhar, author of strangers drowning: Just because she is so influential to me and it was absolutely incredible to interview her :)

There will also be a bonus live Q&A with Financial Planner Cody Garrett who will answer financial planning and tax questions so people can get the help they need asap. 

Together, the speakers will explore everything from how much we can comfortably give and how generosity affects our financial independence plans, to why some charities can accomplish dramatically more with the same donation.

Who is this for?

  • You’re pursuing financial independence and want your money to mean more
  • You want to give more but worry about what it’ll mean for your future
  • You take the standard deduction and want to make the most of the new tax break
  • You itemize but want smarter strategies for charitable giving
  • You want to make generosity a regular value, not just a year-end decision
  • You’re interested in investment strategies that align with pledge-taking and giving meaningful sums of money away

What are we hoping to achieve?

This is an exploration in expanding the top of the funnel for effective giving. Our primary goal is to introduce more people to effective giving and, importantly, turn that awareness into actual donations.

We'll measure success through three key metrics:

  1. The $1,000 Giving Challenge: How many people participate and make a donation they otherwise wouldn't have made. Plus, how many people self-report that they give to more effective charities.
  2. The GiveDirectly Match: How many people participate in the matching opportunity (1.5x), and how much funding does it generate?
  3. The FI-lanthropy Pledge (in partnership with Giving What We Can): How many listeners take the 10% pledge or Trial pledge. We plan to follow up with participants and offer free one-on-one calls to explore making a longer-term giving commitment.

We recognize that self-reported donations won't provide a perfect measure of counterfactual giving, but we hope these results will help us understand whether this type of outreach can encourage more effective generosity when we widen the target to a new audience. 

The summit is free and takes place December 7–8. You can learn more and sign up here.

What this is not

This event is meant to broaden the personal finance world’s exposure to high-impact giving, using language that speaks to them. So we are leading with a carrot, not a stick.

  • We are not excluding people who have charitable interests outside of EA. We are working to expose them to these ideas by bringing their favorite personal finance pros into one space that highlights high-impact giving.
  • We are not positioning effective giving as an all-or-nothing decision. Even small steps toward more impactful giving are worth celebrating at this top of the funnel event.
  • We are not trying to turn the personal finance community into the EA community. We're introducing a new conversation and giving people tools to explore it on their own terms.

We are meeting people where they are at, celebrating progress (not perfection), and creating curiosity. 

Give me your thoughts!

For those of you who have worked on top of the funnel strategy and expanding your reach beyond the center of the target (the existing EA community) - what do you like? What would you change? 

About Me

I’m the founder of Yield & Spread, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that teaches people to build wealth and give it with purpose. I created the FI-lanthropy Pledge, in partnership with Giving What We Can. I’ve helped hundreds of people with their personal finances and giving plans. Yield & Spread has received grant funding from the CEA, and is using part of this funding to support this summit.

item.title: Fish Welfare Initiative’s Funding Gap
item.description:
Published on November 18, 2026 6:44 AM GMT

Fish Welfare Initiative (FWI) works to improve the lives of farmed fish as much as possible. We currently operate in India and China, and are considering expanding to a third country in 2027. We work with species and in contexts where there is little prior welfare research, and so we invest significantly in developing new interventions to suit these contexts.

We now have a relatively large funding gap for 2027 (about $500K of our $1M budget). The rest of this post outlines our work in further detail, and also includes our best case against donating.

If you are interested in supporting our work, feel free to reach out or leave any questions below. As always, we also value feedback from the EA community—we’d love to hear which parts of our strategy seem strong, or which parts seem like they have gaps. Thank you!

About Fish Welfare Initiative

For those who aren’t familiar with FWI, the following are the main things to know:

  • What We Do: We work to improve the welfare of farmed fish, who, like other animals, suffer significantly under modern farming conditions. Our interventions to date have primarily focused on improving water quality.
  • How We Do It: Compared to most animal advocacy organizations, we believe our programs are unusually “on the ground”—we visit fish farms every day to conduct research and work with farmers to make improvements. We also have a particular focus on developing new interventions, given the novelty of this field.
  • Where We Work: We operate in Asia, because this is where about 90% of farmed fish live. To date, we have mostly focused on India, though also with smaller projects in China and the Philippines.
  • Where We Came From: Our illustrious founders, Tom and Haven, took part in the first round of the Charity Entrepreneurship Incubation Program, back in 2019. We were both EA student organizers before that, and have no doubt that FWI would not exist if not for the EA community.

You can get more into the weeds of our organization on our website and our blog.

Our Track Record

Since launching in 2019, we have spent about $3.5M, largely received from donors who would have counterfactually given to other very promising opportunities (this is why we try to be mindful about only raising what we need). In this time and with this money, we believe our key accomplishments have been the following:

  • Direct Impact: We estimate that we have improved the lives of 5.3M fish*, primarily through water quality improvements via our farm program in India.
    • *Note that the magnitude of the welfare benefit to these animals remains somewhat uncertain—we are currently seeking to build a welfare measurement team to address this.
  • Intervention R&D: We have conducted various studies over the years to inform interventions to improve farmed fish welfare. For instance, our recent Sentinel Poles study found a promising way for farmers to detect and treat fish lice earlier, and we are now testing it in a multi-month controlled trial. We primarily do these studies to develop better interventions for our own programming, but also hope that other organizations might some day take up our interventions.
  • Progress in China: Over half of the world’s farmed fish live in China—it is by far the most important country, and among the most complex, in the fish welfare space. While we haven’t run on-the-ground programs in China as we do in India, working with our Chinese partners we have contributed to several firsts (to our knowledge) for fish welfare in the country:
    • China’s first industry report on fish welfare
    • China’s first Aquatic Animal Welfare Forum, which we now co-host regularly
    • China’s first fish welfare standards, which we supported in being developed
  • Movement Support and Indirect Effects: While these should be considered secondary to our more direct outputs, we believe we have also played an important role in building the broader aquatic animal welfare ecosystem. For instance, it is our understanding that our input played an important role in nudging Shrimp Welfare Project to explore corporate advocacy (efforts which later became their Humane Slaughter Initiative), and in launching Scale Welfare and later shaping its strategic direction (e.g. the choice to operate in Vietnam and the Philippines).

Our Latest Plans

We are currently finalizing our next strategic plan, which will shape the direction of our work for the next 3 years. So while we are still finalizing some aspects, the following are the main components of what we are planning:

  • International Expansion: We are now planning to expand beyond India and China, and will likely add a third country of operation in 2027. Depending on our success and capacity, further countries may be added later. We intend to continue focusing on Asia, and our primary contenders right now are the Philippines, Indonesia, Vietnam, and Thailand.
  • Program Growth in India: We plan to expand our farm program in India: in 2027 in our current state (Andhra Pradesh), and to an additional state in 2028. We aim to reach roughly 1,200 farms by 2029 with this expansion (we currently have 195 enrolled in our program).
  • China: We expect our China work in 2027 to focus on developing new interventions with local partners, and on longer-term field building efforts. Further plans are still in development.
  • Continued Applied R&D in India (and other countries): We’ll keep developing new interventions, both through our own studies (e.g. our Sentinel Poles study to address fish lice) and, new for us, by funding others through requests for proposals (RFPs)—starting with our current India RFP and a regional Asia RFP in early 2027. We’ll also scope a new Indian state and new species to learn where interventions are most needed.
  • New, “Systems Change” Style Interventions: We are also exploring investing in indirect, longer-term ways of helping fish. Examples here include corporate outreach, policy work, and supporting other organizations who want to work on fish welfare (e.g. we are considering an on-site “fish welfare fellowship” to train other organizations on how to work with farmers). We are particularly excited about curriculum change—adding fish welfare to the curriculum at fisheries universities and research institutes in India.

Current Funding Gap

We are still in the process of finalizing our 2027 and onwards budgets. However, you can see a preliminary version of them here.

To execute our plans for 2027, we estimate that we will need about $1M. We currently have about $500K raised for 2027, so that puts us at a $500K funding gap for next year (and more for future years). We plan to apply to the usual EA sources, particularly the EA Animal Welfare Fund, to fill part of our gap. However, given the size of our gap, we do think that now is a particularly important time for those interested to donate.

What level of funding would buy different outcomes?

Of course, the reality is that all unrestricted donations go into our general operating budget, but the following are some examples of what different outcomes roughly cost for us to attain:

  • $10: On average, our farm program helps about 10 fish per dollar, so $10 spent on the program helps about 100 fish.
  • $600: A year of water quality monitoring and corrective actions on one farm.
  • $50K: A year of our new Welfare Measurement team, which runs welfare assessment studies on farms inside and outside our program to improve how we measure our impact.
  • $100K: One round of our requests for proposals, funding outside researchers to develop new fish welfare interventions.
  • $125K: A year of Global Growth: scoping new countries in Asia and, if we decide to go ahead in mid-2027, setting up in a third country.
  • $250K: A year of our China work: working with local partners on developing fish welfare improvements, and promoting fish welfare within industry and academia.
  • Beyond our $500K gap: Extra funding would go toward 2028, when we plan to grow in our first new country and expand the farm program into a second Indian state (expected budget about $1.1M).

If you’d like to learn more about donating, see our Donation Page FAQ.

Arguments Against Donating

The following are what I (Haven) currently consider to be the best arguments against donating to our work:

  • Lack of Positive Study Results from R&D Work: Over the past few years, we have run various studies to develop new interventions—specifically on feed fortification, satellite-based water quality monitoring and “chill kill”. We believe that these have been, for the most part, well-run studies, and if there were results to be found, we would have found them. However, to date, most of them have returned negative results (e.g. our feed fortification study surprisingly found no significant welfare benefit of our fortified feed). Our Sentinel Poles study on fish lice is the main exception so far, though it still needs to hold up in a controlled trial. As many of our plans rely on developing new and improved interventions, in India and abroad, this is reason for caution.
  • Cost-Effectiveness: While we believe our programmatic cost-effectiveness is good (our farm program helps about 10 fish per dollar) and is likely among the best in the world in the fish welfare space, it is still lower than what some organizations working on other animals, such as shrimp or chickens, estimate for their own work. For this reason, donors interested primarily in present cost-effectiveness may wish to give elsewhere.
  • Novelty of the Fish Welfare in Asia Space: Farmed fish welfare in Asia is still a very young field. There is extremely sparse research on the welfare issues, and interventions, that affect these animals (this is partly why we invest so heavily in R&D). As a result, much of our work is exploratory and you should likely expect a higher failure rate than in more established areas (e.g. cage-free work to benefit egg-laying hens).

A Note of Gratitude

By haven

Published on November 18, 2026 6:44 AM GMT

Fish Welfare Initiative (FWI) works to improve the lives of farmed fish as much as possible. We currently operate in India and China, and are considering expanding to a third country in 2027. We work with species and in contexts where there is little prior welfare research, and so we invest significantly in developing new interventions to suit these contexts.

We now have a relatively large funding gap for 2027 (about $500K of our $1M budget). The rest of this post outlines our work in further detail, and also includes our best case against donating.

If you are interested in supporting our work, feel free to reach out or leave any questions below. As always, we also value feedback from the EA community—we’d love to hear which parts of our strategy seem strong, or which parts seem like they have gaps. Thank you!

About Fish Welfare Initiative

For those who aren’t familiar with FWI, the following are the main things to know:

  • What We Do: We work to improve the welfare of farmed fish, who, like other animals, suffer significantly under modern farming conditions. Our interventions to date have primarily focused on improving water quality.
  • How We Do It: Compared to most animal advocacy organizations, we believe our programs are unusually “on the ground”—we visit fish farms every day to conduct research and work with farmers to make improvements. We also have a particular focus on developing new interventions, given the novelty of this field.
  • Where We Work: We operate in Asia, because this is where about 90% of farmed fish live. To date, we have mostly focused on India, though also with smaller projects in China and the Philippines.
  • Where We Came From: Our illustrious founders, Tom and Haven, took part in the first round of the Charity Entrepreneurship Incubation Program, back in 2019. We were both EA student organizers before that, and have no doubt that FWI would not exist if not for the EA community.

You can get more into the weeds of our organization on our website and our blog.

Our Track Record

Since launching in 2019, we have spent about $3.5M, largely received from donors who would have counterfactually given to other very promising opportunities (this is why we try to be mindful about only raising what we need). In this time and with this money, we believe our key accomplishments have been the following:

  • Direct Impact: We estimate that we have improved the lives of 5.3M fish*, primarily through water quality improvements via our farm program in India.
    • *Note that the magnitude of the welfare benefit to these animals remains somewhat uncertain—we are currently seeking to build a welfare measurement team to address this.
  • Intervention R&D: We have conducted various studies over the years to inform interventions to improve farmed fish welfare. For instance, our recent Sentinel Poles study found a promising way for farmers to detect and treat fish lice earlier, and we are now testing it in a multi-month controlled trial. We primarily do these studies to develop better interventions for our own programming, but also hope that other organizations might some day take up our interventions.
  • Progress in China: Over half of the world’s farmed fish live in China—it is by far the most important country, and among the most complex, in the fish welfare space. While we haven’t run on-the-ground programs in China as we do in India, working with our Chinese partners we have contributed to several firsts (to our knowledge) for fish welfare in the country:
    • China’s first industry report on fish welfare
    • China’s first Aquatic Animal Welfare Forum, which we now co-host regularly
    • China’s first fish welfare standards, which we supported in being developed
  • Movement Support and Indirect Effects: While these should be considered secondary to our more direct outputs, we believe we have also played an important role in building the broader aquatic animal welfare ecosystem. For instance, it is our understanding that our input played an important role in nudging Shrimp Welfare Project to explore corporate advocacy (efforts which later became their Humane Slaughter Initiative), and in launching Scale Welfare and later shaping its strategic direction (e.g. the choice to operate in Vietnam and the Philippines).

Our Latest Plans

We are currently finalizing our next strategic plan, which will shape the direction of our work for the next 3 years. So while we are still finalizing some aspects, the following are the main components of what we are planning:

  • International Expansion: We are now planning to expand beyond India and China, and will likely add a third country of operation in 2027. Depending on our success and capacity, further countries may be added later. We intend to continue focusing on Asia, and our primary contenders right now are the Philippines, Indonesia, Vietnam, and Thailand.
  • Program Growth in India: We plan to expand our farm program in India: in 2027 in our current state (Andhra Pradesh), and to an additional state in 2028. We aim to reach roughly 1,200 farms by 2029 with this expansion (we currently have 195 enrolled in our program).
  • China: We expect our China work in 2027 to focus on developing new interventions with local partners, and on longer-term field building efforts. Further plans are still in development.
  • Continued Applied R&D in India (and other countries): We’ll keep developing new interventions, both through our own studies (e.g. our Sentinel Poles study to address fish lice) and, new for us, by funding others through requests for proposals (RFPs)—starting with our current India RFP and a regional Asia RFP in early 2027. We’ll also scope a new Indian state and new species to learn where interventions are most needed.
  • New, “Systems Change” Style Interventions: We are also exploring investing in indirect, longer-term ways of helping fish. Examples here include corporate outreach, policy work, and supporting other organizations who want to work on fish welfare (e.g. we are considering an on-site “fish welfare fellowship” to train other organizations on how to work with farmers). We are particularly excited about curriculum change—adding fish welfare to the curriculum at fisheries universities and research institutes in India.

Current Funding Gap

We are still in the process of finalizing our 2027 and onwards budgets. However, you can see a preliminary version of them here.

To execute our plans for 2027, we estimate that we will need about $1M. We currently have about $500K raised for 2027, so that puts us at a $500K funding gap for next year (and more for future years). We plan to apply to the usual EA sources, particularly the EA Animal Welfare Fund, to fill part of our gap. However, given the size of our gap, we do think that now is a particularly important time for those interested to donate.

What level of funding would buy different outcomes?

Of course, the reality is that all unrestricted donations go into our general operating budget, but the following are some examples of what different outcomes roughly cost for us to attain:

  • $10: On average, our farm program helps about 10 fish per dollar, so $10 spent on the program helps about 100 fish.
  • $600: A year of water quality monitoring and corrective actions on one farm.
  • $50K: A year of our new Welfare Measurement team, which runs welfare assessment studies on farms inside and outside our program to improve how we measure our impact.
  • $100K: One round of our requests for proposals, funding outside researchers to develop new fish welfare interventions.
  • $125K: A year of Global Growth: scoping new countries in Asia and, if we decide to go ahead in mid-2027, setting up in a third country.
  • $250K: A year of our China work: working with local partners on developing fish welfare improvements, and promoting fish welfare within industry and academia.
  • Beyond our $500K gap: Extra funding would go toward 2028, when we plan to grow in our first new country and expand the farm program into a second Indian state (expected budget about $1.1M).

If you’d like to learn more about donating, see our Donation Page FAQ.

Arguments Against Donating

The following are what I (Haven) currently consider to be the best arguments against donating to our work:

  • Lack of Positive Study Results from R&D Work: Over the past few years, we have run various studies to develop new interventions—specifically on feed fortification, satellite-based water quality monitoring and “chill kill”. As many of our plans rely on developing new and improved interventions, in India and abroad, this is reason for caution.

For this reason, donors interested primarily in present cost-effectiveness may wish to give elsewhere.
  • Novelty of the Fish Welfare in Asia Space: Farmed fish welfare in Asia is still a very young field. As a result, much of our work is exploratory and you should likely expect a higher failure rate than in more established areas (e.g. cage-free work to benefit egg-laying hens).

A Note of Gratitude

As always, we’d like to note that most of what we’ve been able to accomplish would not have been possible without the incubation, funding, and staff that the EA community has provided. We are extremely grateful for this community, and it continues to be an honor and a pleasure to be a part of it.

item.title: Was I too optimistic about plant-based meat?
item.description:
Published on November 18, 2026 10:25 AM GMT

Cross-posted from my new Substack, Alternative Perspective. Views my own.

Part I of Do Beans Beat Alt Meat?

People know me as a plant-based meat pessimist, mainly for my review “Price-, taste-, and convenience-competitive plant-based meat analogues would not currently replace the majority of meat consumption” (published & free version). I argued that even if products like the Beyond or Impossible burgers were as cheap, tasty and convenient as beef, most people would still choose beef.

However, I ended the paper by claiming “This result does not imply that plant-based meat analogues have no role in environmental, public health or animal welfare policy.” Among other reasons for optimism, I thought that adding a competitive plant-based meat option to a menu might reduce meat consumption, if only by 5 or 10 percentage points. Alas, my own research would show me wrong and wrong again. So in the spirit of caring critique, I will begin with some self-care.

You can see my optimism in predictions I made about the results of a 2023 study. Sagar Shah and I were about to reanalyze 35,048 hypothetical lunch choices by 1,348 university students in Germany. Each student had chosen a meal from a series of lunch menus with five items, two or three of which were meat-free. Some of those meat-free items were plant-based meats, although not the more modern options like Beyond or Impossible. The menus showed photos and descriptions of real university canteen dishes, but no prices.

Before peeking at the data, we wrote out our premonitions. I guessed it was 65% likely that menus with a plant-based meat option resulted in more meat-free choices, and 60% likely that the association would be statistically significant. After conducting our analysis, we found the odds of picking a meat-free option were 1.18 times higher when a plant-based meat was available. So I was “right” on the first one. However, the 90% confidence interval, which accounts for the uncertainty of only asking so many people, ranged from a small drop (0.89) to a large boost (1.56).[1] In other words, I was wrong about distinguishing this result from chance.

Given that the possible range of effects is so wide, the study was inconclusive on this question. I share this study instead to show what I thought at the time. Two subsequent studies have shown me to be wrong more conclusively, although they certainly still have important limitations.

Checked at Chipotle

In a 2026 study led by Jessica Hope (published & free version), we asked 4,431 US adults to pretend to order tacos from Chipotle’s online menu. Each person randomly saw a menu including either one, two or three meat-free options:

  1. Just a veggie filling with guacamole.

  2. Veggie filling + Sofritas, a meaty shredded tofu. (Chipotle’s actual current menu.)

  3. Veggie filling + Sofritas + Chick’nitas, a fictional chicken-style plant-based meat, priced the same as chicken and advertised with a picture of actual chicken.

We hypothesized that each meat-free option added would reduce meat orders. Our study could detect a change as small as a 5-percentage-point drop.

Taco filling choice by menu. Figure 3 from Hope et al. (2026).

But meat orders barely moved. Adding the two options dropped meat orders by 2.1 points, with uncertainty ranging from a 4.4-point decline to a 0.1-point increase. Adding just Sofritas cut meat by 1.1 points (3.3-point decrease to 1.0-point increase). Unlike Chick’nitas, Sofritas is a real product that people have had more than a decade to try! So, despite the name, Hope et al. (2026) did not provide hope for our hypotheses: adding more plant-based meat options mostly pulled people away from the existing veggie option. It ruled out a reduction of 5 percentage points or more.

No change at this register

Of course, that study was hypothetical. While I’d generally expect hypothetical studies to be too optimistic—the stakes are low and people might just try to give the “right” answer—we thought real orders might tell a different story.

In a 2026 study led by Jared Winslow, we analyzed 1.2 million transactions from several restaurants in the US and Canada between 2016 and 2023, which sold 14 plant-based meats. For example:

  1. A burger chain offered the Impossible Burger, Impossible Sausage and Beyond Burger. Its “Gold Standard Impossible” sold 11,000 times, against 94,000 for the “Gold Standard Bacon”.

  2. A breakfast café with an Impossible sausage patty.

  3. A coffee shop and a juice bar with plant-based bacon and sausage.

After introduction, the products accounted for between 1% and 9% of purchases depending on the restaurant, although they cost $1 to $2.50 more than the corresponding meat dishes. Again, we hypothesized that an additional plant-based meat on the menu would decrease meat purchases.

But meat purchases didn’t budge. For three of the restaurants, adding a plant-based meat to the menu had no detectable effect, with uncertainties within ±5%. The other three were much less certain, with some uncertainties ranging from a 21% decrease to a 33% increase. As a result, the overall average is a 1% decrease in meat purchases, but the uncertainty ranges from a 15% decrease to a 16% increase. This wide range shows these six restaurants could not rule out the possibility that plant-based meat works well in some restaurants. But the underlying trend is revealing: for the restaurants where we were more certain, plant-based meat cut meat purchases by less than 5%, if at all.[2] We also analyzed 12 more restaurants with patchier data. With those included, the average was 1% more meat purchases per additional plant-based meat item, with uncertainty between 6% fewer up to 8% more.

There are many other analyses in this paper—including 267 exploratory restaurant-level estimates—that are worth reading: restricting to Impossible products, focusing on repeat customers, or comparing sales before and after each new product launch. However, most result in larger uncertainties. None find particularly compelling results for plant-based meat, although they usually can’t rule out an effect either. The few that stand out could easily be chance, given so many analyses.

Toward realism

Mind you, these are just the studies I worked on since writing my review paper. Among others, that review includes Malan et al. (2022), where Impossible ground beef was added to a university dining hall’s menu and promoted with a climate-themed marketing campaign. Once more, the results point to a small or null effect, within the limitations of the study design. Then there’s the grocery store literature, which I haven’t focused on as much since many plant-based meat products at the grocery store taste bad and cost more. It is nonetheless worth mentioning that studies like Cuffey et al. (2023), Neuhofer & Lusk (2022) and Meyer et al. (2024) also can’t seem to find plant-based meat reducing meat consumption, despite its sales—again with real methodological limitations.

As ever, there is room for skepticism. Only one of the studies was a proper experiment that unequivocally shows causation; maybe the rest were confounded. Maybe the higher plant-based meat prices in some studies drove off customers. Maybe Sofritas, Impossible and Beyond just don’t taste enough like meat. But one certainly has to wonder when study after study can’t find an effect. And we might expect even imperfect products to have some effect. If you dismiss all these results because the products don’t quite achieve “price and taste parity,” I challenge you to fund or conduct the study that does. Taste testing suggests plant-based meats taste better than ever, and prices are readily subsidized within a study. The foretold-yet-ever-elusive impact of competitive plant-based meat could be revealed to us in the present with the right study. For now, I predict another null result.

Although I continue to think that plant-based meat has potential to help animals and our environment, this potential may largely flow through future scenarios where consumer acceptance is much better. Or maybe some regions are already more favorable—these studies are mostly limited to the US. Given these results, we have to ask: do plant-based meats bat above replacement? That is, would consumers prefer another classic plant-based option like beans, falafel or veggies to an alt meat added to a menu? Perhaps these would be seen as more natural, healthy or traditional, or would otherwise find traction. In Part II, we’ll climb the beanstalk...[3]

References

  1. Cuffey, J., Chenarides, L., Li, W., & Zhao, S. (2023). Consumer spending patterns for plant-based meat alternatives. Applied Economic Perspectives and Policy, 45(1), 63–85. https://doi.org/10.1002/aepp.13280

  2. Hope, J. E., Green, S. A., Peacock, J. R., & Mathur, M. B. (2026). Effects of adding plant-based menu options on meat selection frequency: A randomized controlled experiment. Food Quality and Preference, 143, 105931. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodqual.2026.105931

  3. Malan, H., Bartolotto, C., Wilcots, C., Angelis, P., Ferrone, A., Wible, C., Westbrook, E., Fabris, E., Wang, M. C., Slusser, W., Jay, J. A., & Prelip, M. L. (2022). Increasing the selection of low-carbon-footprint entrées through the addition of new menu items and a social marketing campaign in university dining. Journal of the Association for Consumer Research, 7(4), 461–470. https://doi.org/10.1086/720450

  4. Meyer, C., Freitas-Groff, Z., & Woolley, T. (2024). Why are fewer grocery shoppers buying meat? Declining grocery sales, prices, and cultural change (SSRN Scholarly Paper No. 4867295). Social Science Research Network. https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4867295

  5. Neuhofer, Z. T., & Lusk, J. L. (2022). Most plant-based meat alternative buyers also buy meat: An analysis of household demographics, habit formation, and buying behavior among meat alternative buyers. Scientific Reports, 12, 13062. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-16996-5

  6. Peacock, J. R. (2026). Price-, taste-, and convenience-competitive plant-based meat analogues would not currently replace the majority of meat consumption: A narrative review. Appetite, 216, 108301. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appet.2025.108301

  7. Shah, S. K., & Peacock, J. R. (2023). How meat-free meal selection varies with menu options: An exploration. Open Science Framework. https://doi.org/10.31219/osf.io/z8vdu

  8. Winslow, J., Peacock, J. R., Dhargawe, J., Sherman, H., Green, S. A., & Mathur, M. B. (2026). New alternatives, same orders: Modern alternative proteins did not replace meat purchases in restaurants. SocArXiv. https://doi.org/10.31235/osf.io/tpyk9_v1

  1. From here on out, I’ll give ranges for important quantities. These will represent 95% confidence intervals unless otherwise noted. This first one is a 90% confidence interval. ↩︎

  2. Technical note: This paper reports percentage changes, not percentage-point changes. To illustrate the difference, if meat consumption went from 50% to 40%, that would be a 20% decrease (= (50% − 40%) / 50%). It is also a 10-percentage-point decrease (= 50% − 40%). Since my hypothesis was in percentage points, my analysis here in percentages actually favors plant-based meat. The change in percentage points would be smaller. ↩︎

  3. In hopes of learning from a wise hen, of course, not to steal her eggs. ↩︎

item.title: Diversify your giving under uncertainty: Donate through the Cross-Cause Fund
item.description:
Published on November 19, 2026 6:34 PM GMT

TL;DR

Choosing where to give is tough. That’s why we built the Cross-Cause Fund (CCF). It supports high-quality funds in key cause areas and allocates your donation across them using a mathematical model that combines the cost-effectiveness of each option with a range of assumptions about what matters.

As far as we know, this is the most rigorous attempt to prioritize between causes, with transparent modeling that considers multiple moral perspectives, and we recommend using it this Giving Season.

After recent improvements to our approach, the CCF has a new recommended allocation.[1]



 

With a surge of EA-aligned funding expected in 2027, now is a great time to show support for this approach. You can give to the CCF today.

For a quick explanation of the CCF and its underlying model, watch our short video.

Giving responsibly is a challenge

If you try to base your giving on available data and logical reasoning, as most of us in the Effective Giving community try to do, deciding where to give can mean tackling three hard problems at once.

First, you must evaluate available opportunities. As a donor, you often lack comprehensive estimates of the impact of additional funding. For example, organizations may not disclose the level of risk that their projects will fail, or how likely those projects are to secure funding. If you do find estimates, it can be difficult to judge how reliable they are.

Second, you have to figure out what views should influence your giving. Philanthropic interventions can differ in scale, in who is helped, and in how uncertain their benefits are. Even with rigorous cost-effectiveness analysis, it is impossible to compare, say, interventions helping humans with those helping chickens without making a comparative judgment about how much humans and animals matter. It’s tempting to ignore the complexity and make a gut-level decision that reflects unspoken (empirical and normative) assumptions about what matters.

Third, we have to combine hard data with assumptions about what matters to reach a final decision. This is especially difficult when we’re uncertain and want to compare opportunities across different causes: it’s unclear how to act when you have competing views of the world or even how to weigh different options.

The Cross-Cause Fund picks up the challenge

We launched the Cross-Cause Fund (CCF) to take on the challenge of prioritization: dividing resources responsibly across cause areas like global health, animal welfare, AI safety, and so on.

It is built on nearly a decade of Rethink Priorities cause-prioritization research, including projects like Moral Weights, CURVE sequence, CRAFT sequence, Portfolio Builder, and Moral Parliament.

The Fund is a giving vehicle driven by the Cross-Cause Model, a tool that builds a giving portfolio based on hard data plus empirical and normative assumptions about what matters. Even if you have uncertainty about key parameters that matter for the decision, the model can recommend an allocation that accounts for that uncertainty.

 

 

The model allocates money to philanthropic funds vetted by Rethink Priorities. We look for high-quality funds supporting some of the most effective work in their domains. Right now, these funds span Global Health and Development (GHD), Animal Welfare (AW), and Global Catastrophic Risks (GCRS). We plan to expand the list of cause areas in 2027 (current funds list and areas under consideration can be found on our methodology page).

We collect information about the funds, what they have achieved in the past and what they are likely to do with additional funding. From this, we construct cost-effectiveness analyses of each fund. We also estimate how their marginal cost-effectiveness will decline as they absorb more funding.

This still isn’t enough to compare the funds with each other. Some funds help humans, others help animals. Some have effects in the near term, others only in the far future. Some almost certainly create positive impact, while others have a greater risk of causing harm.

The model can evaluate each fund based on a set of assumptions about moral weights of beneficiaries, risk tolerance, attitudes to the far future, and more. We call a full set of assumptions a worldview. Under a single worldview, there is often one cause area (or even a specific fund) that looks the best on the margin.

But most people aren’t fully confident in one worldview. They might be unsure about far-future effects, or how to weight animals on a moral scale. Fortunately, the Cross-Cause Model can allocate funding according to multiple worldviews, making joint decisions about where to give. In this way, we can represent “worldview uncertainty” — with 20% credence in this perspective, say, 30% credence in that perspective, and so on — and get clear guidance on where to give. Accounting for worldview uncertainty can justify splitting funding across causes since different plausible worldviews may favor different allocations. Our model also considers how funds’ marginal cost-effectiveness declines as they absorb more money, which often makes splitting a more attractive strategy.

Collectively, our researchers have spent thousands of hours reasoning about worldview uncertainty. They understand how subjective assumptions interact and how they can be represented in the model, and we ask each of them to record the range of beliefs they find plausible. As they do so, they are able to draw on Rethink Priorities’ body of research on animal moral weights, risk attitudes and far-future effects.

Using the approach set out in our methodology, we aggregate our researchers’ uncertain beliefs to form “house views”: the set of worldviews we use in the model to determine how the Cross-Cause Fund should allocate money. When you give to the CCF, you’re placing trust in this process of explicitly modeling uncertainty.

You can see the CCF evolving in real time

The Cross-Cause Fund is a live tool. Our team of researchers is constantly improving the underlying model and our input estimates with new information as it becomes available. As we make these changes, the giving strategy of the CCF will evolve.

After recent updates, we have new recommended allocations for the CCF fund portfolio.

The allocation changes reflect two broader improvements.

Firstly, we updated our house views. They now include a broader range of moral and empirical inputs, and they represent the views of members of the Cross-Cause Fund research team. The new house views take more seriously the possibility that we cannot reliably tell whether the far future effects of our actions are overall good or bad.[2] As a result, allocations to Global Catastrophic Risk (GCR) decreased. The updated house views also have a stronger emphasis on welfare – of both humans and animals – compared to human life. This led to an increase in the allocation to Animal Welfare funds.

Secondly, we removed limits on how much money each fund can absorb. This resulted in a shift to the Cage-Free Fund, and a shift towards Sentinel Bio and Longview’s Nuclear Fund. We now assume that funds have diminishing returns that tend towards, but do not reach, zero.[3] 

You can find more details about these updates in the forthcoming forum post and our updates tracker.

Transparency is also a core principle of the CCF. We publish our methodology and all updates and improvements made to the model. We’re clear about where the money goes: here is what we did in the first distribution round. Our M&E team develops systems for deciding which funds to add and how to evaluate them. And we share our plans for improving our approach in the future. Right now, we are working on a “Transparency Hub” which will provide all of this information (and more) in a single place. We’re also working on a shareable version of the code for people to review.

We welcome feedback and scrutiny at fund@rethinkpriorities.org.

Who is this for?

The CCF was built for anyone in the effective giving community who wants more rigor and transparency, in both the assumptions and the data used to make giving decisions. If you’re time-poor, this is a good option as your main giving vehicle, or as part of a varied portfolio. If you prefer a hands-on approach to giving, CCF gives you an opportunity to engage with rigorous, transparent reasoning that is open to feedback.

We also think the CCF will be useful as a hedge if your giving is concentrated in one cause area, or guided by a single advisor. You may be more confident than we are about what matters, yet still reluctant to go all-in on a single worldview. Allocating part of your giving through the CCF allows you to account for uncertainty beyond the assumptions guiding your existing donations.

Why now?

With an expected surge in philanthropic funding, this is a pivotal time for the effective giving movement: decisions made now could influence how resources are allocated between causes in the long run.

Donations made through CCF signal support for a rigorous, transparent approach to cause prioritization. Even small donors have a part to play. Your donation can be a vote of confidence in this methodology.

The CCF is an ongoing project that puts our cause prioritization research into action. It’s certainly not perfect. For now, it only spans three cause areas, and the model has room for improvement. We believe the CCF offers a more rigorous way to navigate incomplete information and differing assumptions about what matters than available alternatives, thanks to systematic analysis and explicit modeling. Giving through the CCF this season puts that approach into practice.

Learn more and give

The Cross-Cause Fund is Rethink Priorities effort to take cause prioritization seriously. Our team has created a rigorous methodology, comparing recipient funds side by side on key cost-effectiveness metrics, and we capture uncertainty about key parameters by aggregating the views of our researchers. Crucially, our model puts the two together — hard data and diverse perspectives — to create a giving portfolio that allocates money across causes. And we are committed to constantly improving our approach and to providing transparency along the way.

Now is a pivotal time to support this way of giving. Your contribution can help this approach gain traction, whether the CCF represents a small part of your giving or the whole of it.

Give to the CCF here

Read more on our website.

Thank you to Jim Buhler, M.A. Davis, David Moss, Laura Muresianu, Jonathan Nelson, Carmen van Schoubroeck, and Ula Zarosa for feedback; Ula Zarosa and Francis Priestland for work on the video (made with Claude); and Shane Coburn for editing.

  2. ^

This temporal discount used to entangle one’s views on whether we can counterfactually affect the long-term future at all, whether we can tell in which direction, and simply caring less about future beings. We now have separate wash-out discount and cluelessness discount parameters, and have decided to take for granted that the interests of future beings deserve as much considerations as those of present ones, all else equal (see footnote here). This change makes it easier to accurately model one’s views on the cluelessness thesis, specifically.

  3. ^

     We are still not very confident in our methodology for estimating funds’ diminishing marginal returns curves, and plan to improve them in coming months.
